output.name: Mirrak
output.myth: When Aun cut the string and the sky went up, he was thirsty, as Fliers are, having shouted all day at the wind. Ennu the Kite-Wright sat on the cliff with a goatskin and a needle and said, Fool, you cannot carry water up a cliff with your mouth. So she sewed him a bag from one goat, strap long enough to reach the pasture. Aun slung it on and set off along the Lamp Road. Hirun, the bent-footed gull, circled above him from the north and grumbled that the count was getting wet. Tavo came down the wind, tried the cork, laughed, and could not. The seams held. Some say the bag is still on him, and the stitching shows when the road is long. Kessa, flown from Haskel's Point with a tail to hold a summer, hangs a hand-span south-west and says he has never shared. Grandmother says that is why we sew the seams tight before every journey, and why we never ask the Gale how far. Fill the bag before you go, child. The road is longer than it looks.
output.finding: Find Kessa, the Cut Kite, and look a hand-span to her north-east, where Mirrak hangs on the same Lamp Road.
